intro: Dorian Pâquet’s recording, made on a Chavanne piano dated 2006, offers another way of pacing the E-minor Prelude. The note pattern is spare enough to make small differences of chord balance, release and waiting audible as questions, without assuming which pedal or touch produced them.
question: How does the space before the final chords change the ending’s weight?

sections.label: A′ · Renewed phrase
sections.mNote: the opening shape returns before the final withdrawal

cues.title: Hear the moving middle
cues.text: The repeated chordal accompaniment does not stay harmonically still. Listen between melody and bass for the small shifts that keep the opening moving despite its restrained surface.
cues.evidence: Semitone-based construction and slow melodic motion: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/197. No claim that every voice descends on every chord.

cues.title: A documented modern instrument
cues.text: The source identifies Pâquet’s piano as a Chavanne made in 2006 and dates the recording to 21 October 2019. Those facts describe the instrument and session; they do not by themselves establish an explanation for its recorded tone.

cues.title: Keep the melody separate
cues.text: The upper line can remain almost stationary while the notes beneath it alter the harmony. Try to hear those as separate layers rather than treating each chord as one undifferentiated block.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation grounded in the Prelude’s sparse texture; no particular attack or voicing decision is inferred.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Completion in Mallorca
cues.text: The Op. 28 collection was completed in Mallorca in the winter of 1838–39, using some material conceived earlier. The short E-minor piece belongs to that larger project, not to a securely documented scene or anecdote of its own.

cues.title: Renewal without a new tune
cues.text: The later phrase renews the opening’s basic shape rather than supplying a contrasting middle section. Listen for the changes in harmonic pressure and phrase weight that distinguish the second statement.
cues.evidence: Approximate phrase renewal around0:50, near a report boundary; later activity persists through1:10. Semitone-based phrase design: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/197
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Twenty-four different keys
cues.text: Chopin’s collection moves through pairs of major and relative minor keys around the circle of fifths. The E-minor Prelude follows G major; its identity is one part of a deliberately ordered collection.
cues.evidence: Key ordering described by NIFC: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/12_preludia. This explains the collection, not a musical event at1:25.

cues.title: Wait through the pause
cues.text: The closing region contains a pronounced gap before the final sound. Listen to how that waiting separates the last chords from the earlier recurring pulse; duration alone does not reveal the pianist’s intention.
cues.evidence: Report shows a very low level around1:35 and renewed sounding activity around1:40–1:45. The guide marks the closing region at1:34, not a beat-exact pause boundary.

transitions.title: The opening shape is taken up again
transitions.how: The initial phrase gives way to a renewal of its melodic outline. Repeating the contour does not repeat the whole expressive situation: the inner voices and harmonic continuation intensify the later phrase. Listen for continuity in the melody alongside changes in the support beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Approximate0:50 report boundary supports the phrase-region marker; musical construction: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/197

transitions.title: The recurring pulse yields to a pause
transitions.how: The later phrase withdraws until the recurring accompaniment gives way to a gap. The final chords arrive after this interruption, so the cadence depends on waiting as well as on harmonic resolution.
transitions.evidence: Report’s 1:35 window lies near the noise floor, with renewed sound in the 1:40–1:45 windows; 1:34 is an approximate passage boundary. The waveform supports the gap, but cannot identify an exact release or pedal action.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
